newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea public unaware of defection -- travellers.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea public unaware of defection -- travellers.

text.p: Ordinary North Koreans appear still to be unaware that the ruling communist party's top ideologue defected to South Korea two weeks ago, travellers just back from the isolationist country said on Monday.

And the passengers aboard a scheduled ferry, mainly ethnic Koreans from Japan with relatives in North Korea, said they saw no sign of turmoil over leadership changes or significant food shortages during their visits, mostly to the capital Pyongyang.

The North Korean ferry Mangyongbong 92, carrying 113 passengers, docked on Monday in the Japanese port of Niigata, 260 km (160 miles) northwest of Tokyo, after a 28-hour voyage from the North Korean port of Wonsan.
The ferry, which can carry up to 250 passengers, makes the voyage between the two ports about twice a month.
The passengers, all carrying Japanese passports, had been in North Korea since February 10, two days before top ideologue Hwang Jang-yop sought asylum at South Korea's Beijing consulate.
In possibly the first word from foreign visitors to the Stalinist nation since the defection, passenger after passenger said they had heard nothing in North Korea about the incident.
"There has been no news on the defection," said a 58-year-old woman who visited Pyongyang to attend events to celebrate the 55th birthday of top leader Kim Jong-il on February 16.
Barely a week after the high-profile defection, North Korea announced that ailing premier Kang Song-san had been replaced and that defence minister Choe Kwang had died of a heart attack.
Almost at a stroke, three of the country's top 25 leaders had disappeared from the scene.
Yet visitors saw no signs of a political crisis. "There was absolutely nothing like turmoil in Pyongyang," said the woman, who like all the other passengers, asked not to be identified.
"During my stay in Pyongyang, people were enjoying a quiet life," said a 25-year-old dancer who took part in Kim's official birthday events.
"My relatives there were doing fine. I didn't get even the faintest idea of food shortages," she said.
The comments conflicted with statements by international aid agencies that North Korea is on the brink of a disastrous famine after two years of disastrous floods.
"I did not feel anything strange in Pyongyang," said a 20-year-old singer from the 55-member Korean Art Troupe. "People there, including my relatives, are alive and well."

Washington and Seoul have pledged to send $10 million and $6 million respectively in food aid to North Korea as part of international relief efforts. Japan has so far refused to make a contribution while it investigates media reports that North Korea may have kidnapped some 10 Japanese in recent years.
North and South Korea remain technically at war nearly half a century after their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.
